Reports from support and security about alerts and the inbox:

1. Security: any member can open another member's inbox by changing the address, and can mark another member's alerts as read. Changing another member's notification settings works too.
2. "Mark all read" in one person's inbox clears the unread alerts of everyone else in the workspace.
3. Clicking an alert about an issue opens a page that does not exist. The links in search results and in the daily digest are broken the same way, and the alert about a new member leads nowhere either.
4. Since a recent change, owners are no longer told when someone joins the workspace; the person who joined gets an alert about themselves instead.
5. Assignees are not told when someone else moves their issue to another status, on the board or otherwise.
6. Someone assigned at the moment an issue is created gets no assignment alert; they only get one when assigned later.
7. When the workspace runs out of room on its plan — a project, a seat, an issue, an upload or a webhook endpoint refused — the owner never hears about it.
8. Alerts a member switched off for the inbox still show up there.

Expected behaviour:

- Inboxes and notification settings are personal: a member reads, marks read and configures only their own, whatever their role; anyone else's are refused. Marking all read marks that member's own unread alerts and nothing else. An inbox lists exactly the alerts delivered to it in-app, however many, with no entry duplicated or missing across pages; an alert the member switched off for in-app never appears there, whatever other channels it goes to.
- Every alert and every search hit links to the page the app actually serves. An alert about an issue (assignment, status change, overdue reminder, comment, mention), a search hit for an issue and a search hit for a comment all link to that issue's page in its workspace and project; a search hit for a project links to the project's page; the alert about a new member links to the members settings page; the alert about a full plan links to the billing settings page. Digest entries carry the same links as the alerts they summarise.
- The workspace owner is told when a new member joins; the person who joined is not told about themselves.
- The assignee of an issue is told when somebody else changes its status, including by moving it on the board; nobody is told about their own change, and nothing is sent for an issue that has no assignee. Being assigned at creation is an assignment: the assignee is told exactly as if assigned later, unless they created the issue themselves.
- When a write is refused because the plan has no room for it — another project, another seat (an invitation), another issue in a project, another upload, another webhook endpoint — the workspace owner is told, whoever tried. While that alert is still unread, further refusals for the same resource add nothing; once it has been read, the next refusal produces a new alert. Refusals for different resources are separate alerts. The periodic usage recount, which refuses nothing, never produces one.

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. - git status → "Show working tree status"

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

4	import { and, count, desc, eq, inArray, like } from "drizzle-orm";
5	import { newId } from "@/lib/id";
6	import { getDb, searchIndex } from "@/server/db";
7	import { toIsoTimestamp } from "@/types/common";
8	import { orgPredicate } from "./base-repository";
9	import { compact, keysetPredicate, probeLimit, toPage } from "./_paging";
10	import type { SearchQueryInput } from "@/schemas/search";
11	import type { SearchIndexRow } from "@/server/db/schema/webhooks";
12	import type { OrgId, Page, ProjectId } from "@/types/common";
13	
14	/**
15	 * Upsert by (org, kind, subject) rather than by row id: the indexer is called
16	 * on every write and must be idempotent.
17	 */
18	export async function upsertSearchDocument(
19	  orgId: OrgId,
20	  subjectKind: SearchSubjectKind,
21	  subjectId: string,
22	  content: string,
23	  projectId: ProjectId | null,
24	): Promise<void> {
25	  const db = getDb();
26	  const indexedAt = toIsoTimestamp(new Date());
27	
28	  const existing = db
29	    .select({ id: searchIndex.id })
30	    .from(searchIndex)
31	    .where(
32	      and(
33	        orgPredicate(searchIndex.orgId, orgId),
34	        eq(searchIndex.subjectKind, subjectKind),
35	        eq(searchIndex.subjectId, subjectId),
36	      ),
37	    )
38	    .get();
39	
40	  if (existing) {
41	    db.update(searchIndex)
42	      .set({ content, projectId, indexedAt })
43	      .where(eq(searchIndex.id, existing.id))
44	      .run();
45	    return;
46	  }
47	
48	  db.insert(searchIndex)
49	    .values({
50	      id: newId(),
51	      orgId,
52	      subjectKind,
53	      subjectId,
54	      projectId,
55	      content,
56	      indexedAt,
57	    })
58	    .run();
59	}

61	export async function deleteSearchDocument(
62	  orgId: OrgId,
63	  subjectKind: SearchSubjectKind,
64	  subjectId: string,
65	): Promise<void> {
66	  getDb()
67	    .delete(searchIndex)
68	    .where(
69	      and(
70	        orgPredicate(searchIndex.orgId, orgId),
71	        eq(searchIndex.subjectKind, subjectKind),
72	        eq(searchIndex.subjectId, subjectId),
73	      ),
74	    )
75	    .run();
76	}

78	/**
79	 * Substring match over the denormalised content column. Deliberately simple —
80	 * the index is a convenience layer, not a search engine, and the tenant filter
81	 * is what actually matters here.
82	 */
83	export async function searchDocuments(
84	  input: SearchQueryInput,
85	): Promise<Page<SearchIndexRow>> {
86	  const db = getDb();
87	  const sort = { sortColumn: searchIndex.indexedAt, idColumn: searchIndex.id };
88	
89	  const filters = compact(
90	    orgPredicate(searchIndex.orgId, input.orgId),
91	    like(searchIndex.content, `%${input.q}%`),
92	    input.kinds.length === 0
93	      ? undefined
94	      : inArray(searchIndex.subjectKind, [...input.kinds]),
95	    input.projectId === undefined
96	      ? undefined
97	      : eq(searchIndex.projectId, input.projectId),
98	  );
99	
100	  const total = db
101	    .select({ value: count() })
102	    .from(searchIndex)
103	    .where(and(...filters))
104	    .get();
105	
106	  const rows = db
107	    .select()
108	    .from(searchIndex)
109	    .where(and(...filters, ...compact(keysetPredicate(sort, input.cursor))))
110	    .orderBy(desc(searchIndex.indexedAt), desc(searchIndex.id))
111	    .limit(probeLimit(input.limit))
112	    .all();
113	
114	  return toPage(
115	    rows,
116	    input.limit,
117	    total?.value ?? 0,
118	    (row) => row,
119	    (row) => ({ id: row.id, sortValue: row.indexedAt }),
120	  );
121	}

123	/** Drift alarm input: how many documents this org currently has indexed. */
124	export async function countIndexed(orgId: OrgId): Promise<number> {
125	  const row = getDb()
126	    .select({ value: count() })
127	    .from(searchIndex)
128	    .where(orgPredicate(searchIndex.orgId, orgId))
129	    .get();
130	  return row?.value ?? 0;
131	}

- **Permissions:** notification resources are granted only to their recipient, checked before the role matrix and the platform-staff bypass.
- **Plan-limit alerts:** one alert per resource (title `Plan limit reached for <resource>`). A new one is added only once the previous one is read. The usage recount now emits a separate `billing.usage_warning` event that nothing turns into an alert.
- **In-app filter:** the inbox, bell count, and mark-all-read only consider rows whose channels include `in_app`.
- **Accept-invitation:** the seat refusal there also alerts the owner.

I checked the new behaviour with a temporary test covering each report. It passed (11 cases), and I deleted it afterwards.
